A young man cools off in one of the fountains in Piazza del Popolo, Rome, on Friday 7 August 2026. (Cecilia Fabiano/LaPresse via AP)
- Copyright LaPresse
Nine cities will be under red heat alerts on Friday, while northern regions face a growing risk of torrential rain, hail and strong winds.
The fifth extreme heatwave of the summer has arrived in Italy at the end of August, following a brief spell of unsettled weather that helped bring temperatures down.

According to forecasts, it will not last long, with high temperatures between 27 and 29 August, but it is expected to be the most intense heatwave of the season.
Driven by an African anticyclone, which could also bring Saharan dust, the stifling heat will be concentrated in southern and central Italy, with temperatures reaching 8-10°C above average.
On Thursday, three cities are already under a red alert, according to the latest bulletin from the Health Ministry(source in Italian): Bari, Palermo and Campobasso. Nine cities are on orange alert: Ancona, Cagliari, Catania, Florence, Latina, Messina, Reggio Calabria, Rieti and Rome.
Peak temperatures are expected on Friday and Saturday, especially in the South, Lazio and the central Adriatic regions.
Friday, 28 August, could be the hottest day of summer 2026, with temperatures reaching 45°C in eastern Sicily and 44°C in Puglia. In several inland areas of Calabria, extreme peaks of 45-46°C are forecast.
The heatwave will also affect Sardinia, where maximum temperatures of 44°C are expected, accompanied by "super-tropical" nights when overnight lows on the plains will not fall below 25°C.
On Friday, nine cities will be on red alert: Bari, Cagliari, Campobasso, Catania, Latina, Messina, Palermo, Reggio Calabria and Rome.
In central and southern Italy, temperatures will reach 42°C in Foggia, 40°C in Isernia and 38-39°C in Rome.
The worst of the heat will spare the North, where maximum temperatures are falling, with the Milan area perhaps not even reaching 30°C and Turin at between 27 and 28°C, while the Veneto Plain will see a peak of 34°C.
The north-west will instead be affected by gradually worsening weather. On Friday, the most severe conditions are expected across northern regions, with a risk of torrential rain, hail and strong gusts of wind.
A general improvement and drop in temperatures is expected over the weekend, especially in central and southern Italy. The start of September should remain summery, but between Tuesday 1 and Wednesday 2 September, a new unstable front could move into the north of the country, possibly later involving parts of central Italy. The south will remain warmer.

Weatherwatch: how to protect our railways in hotter summers
Steel rails warping and signalling equipment failing in metal cabinets are among the problems to be solved
Tarmac softens in the summer heat, which may cause problems on the roads, but even trains running on steel rails are not immune.
Railways in the UK are generally designed to operate within a 45C temperature range. The rails expand slightly in the heat, and excessive temperatures can produce “sun kink” with rails warping into S-shapes. The effect is small but the distortion can derail fast trains, so speeds are reduced for safety.
Thermal expansion also causes overhead power lines to droop, and in extreme conditions they may contact trees or other obstacles. This can be solved with auto-tensioning, balancing weights or springs that adjust to changing conditions, but not all power lines have been updated.
Signalling equipment housed in railside metal cabinets is also vulnerable. The inside of these cabinets can reach 70C during a heatwave, causing electronics to fail. Southeastern has been testing IsoMat, a flat aluminium unit that attaches to a signal box and provides cooling. IsoMat is a passive heat exchanger containing sealed internal channels filled with liquid that evaporates and condenses, drawing heat away from the sensitive electronics.
None of these problems are entirely new but they are now more common. Hopefully, hotter summers should drive investment in mitigation measures so that delays due to excessive heat become less rather than more frequent.

Thunderstorms: Île-de-France placed under orange alert this Thursday, August 27.
Published by
My de Sortiraparis · Photos by
My de Sortiraparis · Updated on August 27, 2026 at 02:24 p.m.
Storms are intensifying over Paris and the Île-de-France region this Thursday, August 27, 2026: the area has now been placed under orange vigilance, with a risk of hail and strong gusts expected this afternoon and evening. Here’s the situation.
The situation is tightening in the Paris region. After a sunny morning, Paris (75) and all of Île-de-France’s departments (Yvelines 78, Essonne 91, Hauts-de-Seine 92, Seine-Saint-Denis 93, Val-de-Marne 94, Val-d'Oise 95 and Seine-et-Marne 77) move to orange alert for storms this Thursday, August 27, 2026, according to the latest forecasts from Météo-France. A notch above the yellow level announced earlier in the day, signaling a more virulent outbreak than expected.
In Paris, the day opens under a relatively calm sky. The sun still prevails in the morning, even as high clouds gradually move in. By 8 a.m., the thermometer reads around 19°C, with a light and variable breeze. At first glance, there’s nothing to suggest the weather would deteriorate later on.
The mercury climbs rapidly, reaching about 27°C by around 2 p.m. in the capital. But that rise comes with a clear shift in the weather: cooler air aloft sits atop warm, humid air near the surface — a classic late-summer cocktail that fuels the development of thunderstorm cells, sometimes quite intense.
Hail and gusts up to 65 km/h forecast for Paris
Météo-France forecasts thunderstorms this afternoon, with a pronounced risk of hail. About 5 mm of rainfall is expected over the capital, falling in a very short burst.
The wind can also surge abruptly beneath the storm cells. Gusts up to around 65 km/h are locally possible late this afternoon, enough to make travel uncomfortable and to blow around lightweight street furniture.
The situation remains unsettled this evening. Thunderstorms are expected to affect the region again around 8 p.m., while temperatures hover around 23°C in Paris. Gusts could still reach up to 65 km/h locally this evening and into the early part of the night.
A sweeping storm system hits half the country
Île-de-France is no exception. Météo-France has placed numerous departments on orange alert as the day progressed, the institute highlighting a “new burst of storms” particularly marked from Auvergne to Burgundy and the Vosges, with very intense cells, as well as a second active area stretching from the Pays de la Loire through Normandy to Hauts-de-France.
The alert level has, moreover, been gradually expanded, notably overnight Thursday into Friday as the storm front shifted eastward. To know the real-time alert level for your department, the official Météo-France Vigilance map remains the reference, updated at least twice a day, at 6 a.m. and 4 p.m.
How to stay safe during a thunderstorm?
In the face of this kind of episode, it’s best to postpone outdoor outings. Do not shelter under trees, keep away from rivers, and seek shelter in a sturdy building while the storm cells pass. Météo-France also advises limiting the use of electrical devices and mobile phones during the thunderstorm, and securing objects on balconies and terraces that are exposed to the wind.
This is also the perfect moment to favor indoor activities. Parisian museums and the many current exhibitions offer an ideal refuge to while away the time indoors, just like cinema halls. It could turn a stormy afternoon into a cultural interlude, awaiting the expected lull later tonight into Friday, when the sky should clear and stars return, with temperatures around 19°C by about 2 a.m. If luck is on your side, you might even catch the full moon and the famous lunar eclipse.

title: Extreme heat is taking a toll on firefighters as wildfires stretch crews to the limit - The Conversation

When a wildfire threatens a community, most people don’t think to ask whether the firefighters coming to help slept enough the night before, recovered from the previous day’s shift or have enough energy left for another day on the fire line. They simply expect firefighters to show up.
In conditions like this, the unrelenting heat, stress and smoke take a toll on firefighters’ bodies.
Training, fitness and protective equipment allow firefighters to work in these extraordinary environments. But as a nurse practitioner, firefighter and founder of Purdue University’s FIRE Lab, I know too well that none of that makes the human body’s capabilities limitless.
Heat hits firefighters from 3 directions
Wildland firefighters face heat from the environment, the fire and their own bodies.
Hiking steep terrain with heavy equipment, clearing brush and cutting fire line to stop fires from spreading creates internal metabolic heat. Sun and high air temperatures add environmental heat, while flames and smoldering fuels contribute radiant heat.
The body responds by sending more blood toward the skin to release that heat while continuing to supply oxygen to working muscles. The heart works harder to support both jobs.
As fluid losses increase, the volume of blood circulating through the body can fall, the heart rate rises, and the work of fighting fires feels harder.
Field studies show how this strain can become severe. In one study of 221 wildland firefighters on the job, 61% reached a core temperature of at least 100 F (38 C). About 50% reached a physiological strain index of 6 or greater on a 0-to-10 scale that combines heart rate and core temperature to measure how hard the body is working to cope with heat. Among those whose body temperatures crossed 100 F, the majority remained above that temperature for more than 30 minutes.
A core temperature of 100 F does not by itself mean heat stroke, but it signals substantial physiological strain. Staying hydrated helps the body sweat and keep blood circulating, but even a fully hydrated firefighter can overheat when the body gains and produces heat faster than it can release it.
Immediate consequences can develop quickly
Heat strain may begin with fatigue, headache, dizziness, weakness or nausea and progress to heat exhaustion or heat stroke. Severe hyperthermia can affect the brain, heart, kidneys and liver.
Wildland firefighters can also face rhabdomyolysis, a breakdown of skeletal muscle that can contribute to kidney injury. The National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health reported 62 severe cases among wildland firefighters from 2010 to 2020 and cautioned that the true number was probably higher.
Heat adds to fatigue when firefighters must anticipate fire behavior and make rapid decisions.
A 2025 field study found that wildland firefighters averaged 13.8-hour shifts on days when they were fighting fires and got around 6.7 hours of sleep. Poorer sleep and longer shifts were associated with reduced cognitive function, which can affect a firefighter’s ability to make split-second calls, such as when to retreat from an escalating fire.
Effects stay with bodies beyond one shift
The effects of heat and exhaustion can also add up. A firefighter can finish a shift hot, smoke-exposed and physically depleted, sleep in a warm camp and return to the line before fully recovering. Repeating that pattern across days and fire seasons may place ongoing strain on the heart, lungs and kidneys.
Smoke adds another health risk. Wildland firefighters commonly work in smoke without the kind of protection that firefighters use when fighting blazes inside buildings.
A 2019 exposure-modeling study estimated that, depending on the number of fire days worked over a career, cumulative smoke exposure could increase a wildland firefighter’s risk of dying from lung cancer by 8% to 43% and dying from cardiovascular disease by 16% to 30%. These are estimates, but they show why career-long exposure deserves attention.
Kidney health is another emerging concern. A 2025 study of 39 wildland firefighters found temporary decreases in kidney function and changes in kidney-injury biomarkers during one midseason fire incident. More research is needed to determine whether firefighting over seasons and years can lead to persistent kidney damage.
These findings raise an important occupational health question: What happens when heat, dehydration, smoke, sleep disruption and extreme physical exertion accumulate not only across one incident but across an entire career?
How to lower the risk
The heat isn’t going away, but there are ways wildfire management agencies can reduce the risk to firefighters.
First, firefighter health should be an important part of national wildfire readiness policies. Having adequate staffing so firefighters aren’t overworked and have meaningful enough recovery time to rehydrate, cool down and sleep between shifts are important. So are conditions that allow real sleep between shifts.
Monitoring firefighters’ health can also help catch early warning signs, such as kidney stress or burnout.
The public can also help by reducing the likelihood of high-stress fire situations.
The National Interagency Fire Center estimates that about 85% of U.S. wildfires are caused by human activities. Some of those can be avoided by fully extinguishing campfires, checking local fire restrictions, avoiding spark-producing activities on dry, windy days when fire risk is high, and maintaining vehicles and trailers so metal does not drag and ignite vegetation.
If you live in wildfire-prone country, creating defensible space and reducing combustible material around your home can reduce the fuel for fires. Evacuating promptly in an emergency also reduces the likelihood firefighters will have to put themselves in high-stress situations to rescue you.
We all expect firefighters to be there when the worst happens. Making sure they can do their jobs and stay healthy will allow them to continue to show up.

full_text:
Water levels in the main reservoirs supplying the capital Tegucigalpa have become worrying. Photo: EFE.
August 27, 2026 Hour: 12:13 am
The Government of Honduras reported this Wednesday that 28 new municipalities are under red alert as a result of the drought associated with the El Niño phenomenon. The measure follows a decree issued Tuesday that established an indefinite red alert for 75 localities. The new additions bring the total number of municipalities under emergency to 103.
Affected areas span the departments of Comayagua, La Paz, Francisco Morazán, El Paraíso, Valle, Choluteca, Intibucá and Lempira, located in the center, east, south and west of the country.
An estimated 10.5 million people in the Central American Dry Corridor have been impacted, with many engaged in subsistence farming of corn and beans and dependent on seasonal rains for both production and food supply.
RELATED: El Niño Raises Heat, Drought and Cyclone Risks in Cuba
Water levels in the main reservoirs supplying the capital Tegucigalpa have become worrying, prompting authorities to tighten water rationing.
According to the Secretariat of Risk Management and National Contingencies (Copeco), another 82 municipalities are under yellow alert and 48 remain under preventive green alert. The agency said the delayed rainy season caused accumulated precipitation deficits of between 100 and 200 millimeters, affecting water availability for human and animal consumption.
The National Center for Atmospheric, Oceanographic and Seismic Studies (Cenaos) stressed that hotter and drier than normal conditions persist, associated with a strong El Niño event. A temperature increase of 0.5 to 1 degree was expected between March and August, with the greatest impact in the southern part of the country.
United Nations resident coordinator in Honduras, Alejandro Álvarez, announced new aid of 20 million dollars to mitigate the effects of the climate emergency.

LAFAYETTE, La. (NEWS 15) — Acadiana is back under a Heat Advisory after a one-day reprieve, with the heat index climbing into the triple digits and feels-like temperatures reaching up to 110 degrees.
Experts advised residents to drink plenty of water and avoid unnecessary exertion on days with extreme heat.
Outdoor workers in Lafayette described how they are coping with the excessive heat.
"I feel like it's getting hotter and hotter," Damon Thibodeaux and Darren Wiliams said. "The last couple months, it's been super hot. The best advice I could give is to stay hydrated. Cool off as much as you need because it drops a lot of people, but I'm used of it, man, and it's possible. This is what I love doing, and I do it good."
Acadiana residents are expected to continue facing elevated heat index values as the advisory remains in effect.
